candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classified this binary as malware with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, with SHAP contributions from +0.0059 to +0.0113. No n-gram in the evidence offsets this. The n-grams fall into two groups that fit hash-based proof-of-work mining. The first is rotate and bit-manipulation sequences: ADD ROR (+0.011316), ROL AND (+0.008735), MOV ROL (+0.008407), ROL ADD (+0.007307), ROL MOVZX (+0.006792), XOR ROL (+0.006662, the most frequent at 0.004449), SHL OR (+0.007609), BSWAP LEA (+0.006759), and the carry-chain pairs SUB ADC (+0.008808) and ADC XOR (+0.006348). Dense rotate/XOR/add mixing is typical of hash round functions such as those in CryptoNight-style or similar mining algorithms. BSWAP suggests endianness conversion of hash state. The second group is SSE2 vectorized data movement and mixing: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.011041), MOVHLPS MOVQ (+0.009378), ADD MOVQ (+0.009308), PXOR PXOR (+0.008101), MOVDQA PAND (+0.006796), PADDQ MOVDQA (+0.006575), LEA PXOR (+0.006193), MOVDQA PXOR (+0.006004), and MOV PUNPCKLQDQ (+0.005919). These suggest 128-bit XOR, AND, and 64-bit add operations on wide state blocks, consistent with scratchpad or state-mixing loops. The evidence has no function names, API calls, or strings, so the case rests on instruction-level patterns. Many individual n-grams are also common in legitimate cryptographic or compression code. Even so, the breadth of agreement across 20 independent features, the very high model probability, and the combination of rotate-heavy integer mixing with SSE2 state manipulation make a mining-style compute kernel the most plausible reading.
